metadata.title: Teacher job satisfaction: International evidence on the role of school working conditions and teacher characteristics

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2019 teacher questionnaire data for grade 8 mathematics teachers across 46 participating education systems and benchmarking entities. The TIMSS sampling design is described as two-stage cluster stratified sampling with PPS school sampling and intact-class sampling, and teacher responses are collected for the target grade. The authors explicitly state they did not use teacher weights because the analysis is at the teacher level and focuses on teacher characteristics and school working conditions rather than student-level outcomes. No replicate-weight method (e.g., BRR/jackknife) is reported, and the manuscript does not name any teacher weight variable, so weighting for complex survey design is not incorporated in the reported regression models.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: plausible_values_handling is 'not_applicable' — the study likely does not analyze cognitive achievement PVs (e.g., it may focus on affective/attitudinal outcomes, curriculum data, or non-ILSA micro-data).

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TIMSS 2019 teacher questionnaire data for grade 8 mathematics teachers only. The analytic sample is restricted to teachers in participating countries/benchmarking entities with complete data on the items used to construct the latent scales (teacher job satisfaction, teacher workload, student discipline, and the single-item leadership support), with listwise deletion applied because item-level missingness was about 10% and the authors retained only complete cases. The study does not include school- or classroom-level variables and treats each teacher response as an independent observation in the regression stage.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics teacher questionnaire (46 education systems)
main_findings.target_variable: Teacher job satisfaction (latent scale; affective items)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Pooled regression (standardized estimates): Leadership Support 0.266***; Student Discipline 0.356***; Teacher workload −0.113***; Gender 0.071**; Teaching years −0.006***; Mathematics 0.023 (ns); Mathematics education −0.029 (ns); PD 0.084***. Model fit/scale validation reported via CFA fit indices (e.g., Job satisfaction CFI=0.995, TLI=0.987, RMSEA=0.065, SRMR=0.010).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics teacher questionnaire the study leveraged leadership support, student discipline, teacher workload, teacher gender, and professional development hours to model teacher job satisfaction, finding that leadership support and student discipline were positively associated with job satisfaction while teacher workload was negatively associated (and professional development was positively associated). This indicates that strengthening school leadership support and improving classroom discipline—along with reducing excessive teacher workload—may be effective levers for improving teacher job satisfaction, though the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.

data.outcome_summary: The study conducts a secondary analysis of TIMSS 2019 teacher questionnaire data for grade 8 mathematics teachers across 46 education systems/benchmarking entities (N=13,048 teachers). Teacher job satisfaction is measured as an affective latent construct from five recoded items, with CFA-based scale validation and multi-group measurement invariance testing; metric invariance was achieved, enabling comparisons of associations (but not mean levels). In pooled regression models, leadership support (β=0.266***), student discipline (β=0.356***), and professional development hours (β=0.084***) were positively associated with job satisfaction, whereas teacher workload (β=−0.113***) and teaching years (β=−0.006***) were negatively associated; gender showed a small positive association (β=0.071**). Country-specific regressions show cross-national variation in significance and direction, especially for workload. The analysis uses listwise deletion for item missingness (~10%) and does not apply teacher weights, so results may be sensitive to complex survey design and to the cross-sectional, self-report nature of the measures.
